question.explanation:
Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block $J_n(\lambda),$ we have \[ f(J_n(\lambda)) = \begin{bmatrix} f(\lambda) & f'(\lambda) & \dfrac{f''(\lambda)}{2!} & \cdots & \dfrac{f^{(n-1)}(\lambda)}{(n-1)!} \\ 0 & f(\lambda) & f'(\lambda) & \cdots & \dfrac{f^{(n-2)}(\lambda)}{(n-2)!} \\ \vdots & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 0 & \cdots & 0 & f(\lambda) & f'(\lambda) \\ 0 & \cdots & \cdots & 0 & f(\lambda) \end{bmatrix}. \]

In this case, we have $f(x) = \sin {3x},$ $n=2,$ and $\lambda=\dfrac{\pi}{6}.$

Since $n=2,$ we need to compute the first $2-1=1$ derivative of $f{:}$

\begin{align*} f(x) &= \sin{3x} \\[5pt] f'(x) &= 3\cos{3x} \\[5pt] \end{align*}

Therefore, we have

\begin{align*} f\left(J_2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\right) &= \begin{bmatrix} f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) & f'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) \\ 0 & f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} \sin \left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) & 3\cos \left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \\ 0 & \sin \left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{1} & \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{0} \\ \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{0} & \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{1} \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] \end{align*}

question.text:
Consider the following matrices:

\[ E = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{\pi }{6}& 0 \\ \dfrac{5\pi }{6}&\pi \end{bmatrix}, \qquad D = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{\pi }{6} &0 \\ 0 & \pi \end{bmatrix}, \qquad P = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \]

Given that $E = PDP^{-1},$ find $4\sin E.$
question.explanation:
Given a function $f$ and matrices $A$ and $S,$ where $S$ is invertible, we have \[ f(SAS^{-1}) = S \cdot f(A) \cdot S^{-1}. \]

For $f(x) =4\sin E$ and the given matrix $C,$ we have

\[ 4\sin E = 4\sin (PDP^{-1}) = P \cdot (4\sin D) \cdot P^{-1}. \]

Now, since $D$ is a diagonal matrix, we get

\[ 4\sin D = \begin{bmatrix} 4\sin \dfrac{\pi }{6} & 0\\ 0 & 4\sin \pi \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Also, the inverse of $P$ is

\[ P^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{1\cdot1 - (-1)\cdot 0} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Therefore, we conclude that

\begin{align*} 4\sin E &= P \cdot (4\sin D) \cdot P^{-1} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} {2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1& 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 2&0\\ 0&0 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 2&0\\ -2&0 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}
